huro-lst-0236.history: The Episcopal Society of Huron was organized in 1837 under the Rev. F. M. Levenworth, and the cornerstone of the present building was laid on 23 May 1838 — making it the oldest church building in Huron, standing near what had been the original southern limit of the village. The Rev. Samuel Marks became pastor in 1839 and served for over forty years. The building was added to the National Register of Historic Places on 4 March 1975 (reference no. 75001379), and the congregation marked its sesquicentennial in 1988.
huro-lst-0236._history_sources: Sentences 1-3 are a close paraphrase of the Huron Historical Society marker transcription; sentence 4's NRHP date and reference number are from the Wikipedia article's NRHP infobox.

huro-lst-0035.history: Huron's fire service was established in 1860 with hand-pumped equipment. In 1915 the village bought a horse-drawn ladder wagon from the City of Elyria, and local horse owners raced their teams to the station when the alarm sounded. Hank Schaffer was appointed the first fire chief in 1920 at $50 a year. Steam whistles served as the fire signal until 1923, when the city bought an electric siren for about $350. The first motorised apparatus, a Buffalo Larrabee pumper, arrived in 1925, followed by a Mack truck in 1934 that its crews nicknamed the "Blue Goose" for its blue paint. The division hired its first full-time firefighters in 1969 and bought its first ambulance the same year. In 1974 the station moved from the corner of Main Street and Jim Campbell Boulevard to the north end of Main Street. A fire levy in 1986 paid for four more full-time members and a 22-foot Boston Whaler rescue boat.
huro-lst-0035._history_sources: Every sentence is from the division's own history page; dates and figures are as published there. I left out the 2000 Twine House fire, the 1999 thermal-imaging purchase and the chief succession (2003/2008/2009/2026) — recent operational detail rather than the building's story.

huro-lst-0195.history: BGSU Firelands was established in 1968 as Bowling Green State University's regional campus, about 60 miles north-east of the main Bowling Green campus, and it remains the university's sole regional campus. Its first dean was Dr. James H. McBride. When the campus was being developed in the late 1960s, McBride and his wife Margaret saw that the college held over 250 acres while only about a third was needed for buildings, and argued that the remainder "should be beautified for the edification, enjoyment, and education of all who would come." That became the James H. McBride Arboretum, established in 1983 as a partnership between BGSU and Erie Metroparks and named for him; it now holds over 200 species of flowers, trees and shrubs, with restored prairie plots, walking paths around Parker Lake and trails along Sawmill Creek.
huro-lst-0195._history_sources: Sentence 1 from the About page; sentences 2-4 from BGSU's McBride Arboretum page, with the McBride quotation reproduced as that page gives it.
huro-lst-0195.description: Bowling Green State University's regional campus, on a 250-acre site at One University Drive. One of BGSU's seven undergraduate colleges and its only campus outside Bowling Green, it teaches applied sciences, humanities, natural and social sciences, and College Credit Plus, and hosts outside events in its meeting spaces, auditoriums and the McBride Arboretum.
